title: Belief that Progress has Been Made in Curing Cancer Varies by Perception of Social Media Health Mis- and Disinformation, Education, Frequency of Social Media Use, and Healthcare System Trust: A Cross-Sectional Study
screen_reason: The paper's aim is a belief outcome (progress in curing cancer), which on its own would be excluded, but its sample description (Table 1) reports the survey-weighted distribution of the HINTS 6 (2022) item 'How much of the health information that you see on social media do you think is false or misleading?': 36% of 4,246 adult social media users answered 'a lot' ('substantial'). That is a share of respondents reporting a perceived amount of misinformation in their information environment, which counts as RECALL. All other results (odds ratios, predicted probabilities of believing in cancer progress) are belief outcomes and give no rows.

estimates.measure_type: % of adult social media users who think that 'a lot' of the health information they see on social media is false or misleading
estimates.denominator: 4,246 adult social media users in HINTS 6 (2022), a nationally representative US survey of non-institutionalised adults 18+; percentages are survey-weighted (jackknife replicate weights). Respondents who reported not using social media (N = 1,211) and cases with missing data (N = 713) were excluded
estimates.definition: respondent answered 'a lot' to 'How much of the health information that you see on social media do you think is false or misleading?'; 'a lot' was coded 'substantial', while 'none', 'a little' and 'some' were coded 'less than substantial'
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation refers to false or misleading information shared unintentionally, while disinformation denotes the deliberate creation and dissemination of false information"; the measure itself asks about health information that is "false or misleading"

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Entirely respondent-judged perception of how much of the health content they see is false or misleading; no verification of any item. HINTS 6 is administered by the National Cancer Institute by mail and online, March-November 2022, response rate 28.1%; analysis used survey weights and jackknife replicate weights.
estimates.moderator_quote: you see on social media do you think is false or misleading?
estimates.notes: The 36% is the top ('a lot') category only: the paper's dichotomy merges 'none', 'a little' and 'some' into '< substantial' (64%), so no broader 'any perceived misinformation' share can be recovered from the published tables. Denominator is social-media users, not all US adults - 1,211 non-users were dropped - so this is a share of the social-media-using population. The 36% in the last two columns of the same table row is the cross-tabulation with the cancer-progress outcome (18% + 18%), not part of this estimate.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) the outcome variable distribution (54% believe progress has been made in curing cancer, 46% not) - a belief about cancer, not misinformation. (b) All odds ratios (e.g. OR = 0.74 for perceiving substantial mis/disinformation) and all predicted probabilities of believing in progress (60%, 53%, 42%, 36%, 62%, 55%, 44%, 53%, 55%, 60%, 59%) - these are belief outcomes conditional on perceived misinformation, not exposure shares. (c) The Table 1 cross-tabulation cells (e.g. 18%/18% for the 'substantial' row) - they are joint percentages of the belief outcome, not the exposure prevalence. (d) All demographic distributions in Table 1. (e) Any 'any perceived misinformation' figure - unavailable because 'some' is merged into the '< substantial' category.

rob.design: Secondary analysis of HINTS 6 (2022), a nationally representative mail/online survey of non-institutionalised US adults 18+ run by the National Cancer Institute; field period March-November 2022; response rate 28.1%. Analytic sample restricted to social media users after excluding 1,211 non-users and 713 cases with missing data by listwise deletion, leaving 4,246; all estimates survey-weighted with jackknife replicate weights, analysed in Stata 18.5, STROBE-compliant reporting. The misinformation measure is a single self-report perception item dichotomised at 'a lot', with no external verification and no reliability statistics; the dichotomisation follows prior studies. Cross-sectional design, so no causal claim about exposure. Listwise deletion and the exclusion of non-users limit generalisability to the social-media-using adult population.
